newsitem.title: USA: U.S. calls for new UK 'open skies' air talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. calls for new UK 'open skies' air talks.

text.p: The United States has called for a resumption of its long-stalled "open skies" aviation negotiations with Britain, starting in December, the U.S. Transportation Department said Thursday.
The U.S. announcement followed two days of informal talks in Washington Wednesday and Thursday. The talks had been held to see if there were grounds to resume negotiations.

"There was a useful exchange of views leading to a better understanding of each country's concerns," the department said in a statement, "and the two countries will consult regarding the resumption of formal negotiations."
The United States suggested the negotiations be held Dec. 4 to 6 in London. British officials said those dates would be reviewed by authorities in London.

U.S.-British negotiations on an "open skies" free market aviation accord to replace their existing highly restrictive accord have been on and off for two years, with the latest round collapsing last August.

The United States envisions an "open skies" accord as one that allows an airline of one country to fly to all cities it wishes in the other country, with rights to pick up passengers and fly to countries beyond.

Washington broke off the negotiations in August, saying London was unwilling to negotiate. U.S. officials have repeatedly cited Britain's reluctance to cede additional slots at congested London Heathrow airport to U.S. carriers.
Service to Heathrow, where British Airways has 38 percent of the slots, is considered vital for U.S. carriers who want to carry passengers beyond to continental Europe.
Under the current pact, only two U.S. carriers, American Airlines and United Airlines, have landing rights at Heathrow, and authority to fly beyond is highly limited.
Washington called for the informal talks held here the past two days, but gave no indication just what "better understanding" was gained in them to warrant a resumption of formal negotiations.
Industry sources said an impetus might have come from British Airways and American Airlines, who are seeking U.S. government approval for a marketing alliance on transatlantic services.
Such an alliance would need immunity from U.S. antitrust law, and Washington has said that such immunity would not be granted without an "open skies" pact first agreed to.
